pages.intro:
A student-run lab for ASIC and FPGA hardware verification. We exist because the tools, the boards and the mentorship are hard to get to alone — so we pool them, run real RTL through real flows, and publish everything we learn.

No coursework. No spectators. You take a block, you verify it, you sign it off.

sections.heading: INK · FIVE FRAMES
sections.kicker: MARK ── FIVE STAGES OF STANDING UP

sections.body:
He stands at the end of the pipeline and nothing gets past him unsigned. Not a block, not a bitstream, not a waiver somebody talked themselves into late on a Friday. If it has not been verified, it does not ship, and the person who wrote it is the one who has to say so out loud.

Timing closure has a price, and it is always paid in something you liked. A stage you were proud of gets retimed. A clever optimisation comes out because it cannot be proven. A constraint file gets read for the fourth time at midnight, and the fourth reading is the one that finds it.

We keep the plate on the wall because that price is the actual work. Everything else is waiting for a run to finish.

sections.body: A TCP/IP stack implemented entirely in FPGA fabric. MAC, ARP, IPv4, the RFC 9293 state machine, retransmission, RTO estimation, congestion control and reassembly are all RTL.
sections.heading: $ cat README.md | head

sections.body:
application (echo | counter)
               │
       toe_tcp_engine     RFC 9293 FSM, cwnd,
               │          retransmit, reassembly
       toe_ip_bridge      header + RFC 1071 csum,
               │          double-buffered
         eth_ip_core      IPv4 + ARP + MAC
               │
     gig_ethernet_pcs_pma  SGMII
               │
      GTH Quad 225 ch2 ──▶ SFP0 cage
sections.heading: THE STACK

items.detail: The application writes into toe_send_buffer. On a flush the engine asks toe_segmenter for a segment bounded by cwnd, the peer window and free retransmission-table space. The bridge builds the header and computes the checksum while it reads, over a doubled buffer so segment N+1 is prepared while N is on the wire.
items.label: TX PATH

items.detail: The bridge parses inbound TCP, verifies the checksum and offers it to the engine. A one-deep skid buffer latches it the cycle it is offered, whatever the FSM state. Pure ACKs drain even while the FSM waits on a TX segment.
items.label: RX PATH

items.value: rtl/ 23 VHDL modules · rtl/eth/ 28 Verilog files · tb/ 49 testbenches · vectors/ 25 golden files

sections.body:
00:0a:35 is the Xilinx OUI; bc:e9:2f is the host NIC. Two distinct MACs, not loopback. Taking the host link down mid-transfer halted the stream at once, and every source in build_toe.tcl greps clean for zynq_ultra_ps_e, processing_system and PS8.

Passive open now works too: 40 of 40 sequential inbound connections accepted.

items.detail: Start the checksum at accept time and feed it words as bytes arrive, overlapping the ~740-clock walk with the 1460-clock read.

Single connection: no session table. RFC compliance measured on the wire is 10 PASS / 2 FAIL. Regression runs 46 pass / 2 fail / 1, both failures pre-existing on baseline RTL.

WIN_LIMIT is a deployment constant at 8192; raising it to 32768 changed nothing, because the board is the sender. Bouncing the host NIC can drop the SGMII carrier; budget one reflash after any link interruption.

sections.body: Two messengers for the grid. An IEEE C37.118.1 phasor measurement unit that reports six channels at 50 frames a second, and an IEEE 2664-2024 (STTP) publisher that carries the same measurements over TCP with no processor anywhere in the datapath.
sections.heading: Power System Protocols

images.alt: A pigeon messenger in a red cap carrying a satchel

sections.body:
A PMU samples the grid's voltages and currents, turns each cycle into a phasor (magnitude, angle, frequency, rate of change) and stamps it with GPS time. The PMU is the pigeon: it writes the letter. The protocol is how the letter travels.

C37.118 is the classic fixed-frame carrier. STTP is the newer one: it compresses the measurements with TSSC and negotiates a subscription over TCP. Both are built here on the same ZCU106 board.

sections.body: on the flight of many machines, and how they keep from striking one another
sections.heading: Codex of the Swarm

images.alt: Leonardo's aerial screw
images.caption: Fig. A — the aerial screw. One rotor lifts one machine; this codex concerns many.

sections.body: A ROS 2 and PX4 SITL multi-drone swarm package. It spans single-drone offboard control through to decentralised formation flight, area-coverage missions, collision avoidance and leader-failure reassignment, all driven from a single YAML config and one ros2 launch invocation. It speaks to PX4 through uXRCE-DDS and px4_msgs, not MAVROS.
sections.kicker: Every result below is simulated, in Gazebo Harmonic 8.11.0 with PX4 SITL. No real-hardware flight has ever been performed. Where the README and the claims matrix disagree, the matrix is right.

sections.body:
Three machines rise in a triangle: one leader at the origin, two followers set three paces behind and three to either side. The leader walks its path fifteen metres out and back at five metres' height; the followers keep station in its frame.

Should the leader fall silent, each follower names the lowest-numbered peer still speaking. Every drone reaches the same answer from its own view, and no council is needed.

sections.body: INIT → ARM_OFFBOARD → FLY → LAND → DONE. Arming waits for 25 ticks of stable OFFBOARD.

items.label: Forced collision

images.alt: Ink drawing of a swarm of craft descending over a lone figure
images.caption: Plate I — many craft, one sky. The question of Liber II is what happens when their messages arrive late.

sections.body: Three layers keep the machines apart: a clamp holding each setpoint 2.5 m from any peer, a quadratic repulsive velocity up to 4 m/s inside 1.5 m, and a full halt below 0.6 m. Across 98 nights, from 18 May to 24 August 2026, ten fault scenarios were injected and every surviving log re-parsed.
sections.heading: Of Near Collisions
Fig. C — Worst Separation by Scenario
Fig. D — Runs Below the Hard Floor (1.0 m)

sections.body:
64 of 2,852 completed runs fell below 1.5 m and 37 below 1.0 m; the worst came within 0.22 m. 33 of the 37 hard-floor breaches sit in two scenarios, dds_loss_5 and dds_delay_50.

All three layers read peer position. Degrade the transport and the clamp clamps against stale data, repulsion pushes from a phantom, and the halt never arms.
sections.heading: The Flaw, Honestly Kept

sections.body: Under CPU stress at two cores, 441 runs recorded 0 violations with a worst separation of 1.52 m. Leader and follower kills recovered through decentralised reassignment.

sections.body:
A six-channel interpolated-DFT front end for grid instrumentation. Each channel windows its input, runs a sliding DFT bin, extracts magnitude and phase with a CORDIC, and differentiates frequency to get ROCOF. One clock domain, fixed point throughout, no vendor IP.

It exists because a commercial PMU front end costs more than the lab's annual budget, and because it is a good excuse to learn where a fixed-point error budget goes wrong.
sections.heading: POWER SYSTEM PROTOCOLS

sections.body: IN VERIFICATION
sections.heading: BUILD.STATUS

items.detail: Hann coefficients in a single BRAM, shared across channels by time multiplexing. Q1.15 in, Q2.30 out, truncation error bounded at 2⁻¹⁴.
items.label: STAGE 1

items.detail: Recursive bin update with leakage damping, five bins per channel. Guard bits sized from the worst-case input rather than from optimism.
items.label: STAGE 2

items.detail: 16-iteration vectoring CORDIC, one shared engine, arctan table in ROM. Gain compensated at the output, not per iteration.
items.label: STAGE 3

items.detail: Three-point interpolation over neighbouring bins to recover off-bin frequency, then a differentiator for ROCOF with a configurable window.
items.label: STAGE 4
ROCOF step response vs. golden model

sections.body: ROCOF overshoots by 4.2 % on a 2 Hz/s step when the differentiator window is 4 samples. Suspected guard-bit truncation in stage 4.
